newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Aeroflot pens deal to buy "Russian-American" jets.
newsitem.headline: Aeroflot pens deal to buy "Russian-American" jets.

text.p: Russia's Aeroflot airline on Tuesday signed a $1.5 billion deal to buy 20 Russian jets equipped with American engines and electronics, a move officials hope will help revive the faltering domestic aviation sector.
"This marks the rebirth of Russian aviation," said Yuri Kolesnikov, a senior government adviser on defence industries.
"It is important for Russian aviation to be integrated with different technologies and this deal joins Russian aviation with the world community."

Under the agreement, signed at Aeroflot Russian International Airlines' Moscow headquarters, the Voronezh Jet Construction company will build the IL-96 M/T planes and equip them with Pratt & Whitney engines and electronics made by Rockwell Avionics.
The new jets are part of an expansion by Aeroflot, which inherited the foreign routes of the Soviet airline and is now seeking to modernise its aging fleet.
It already operates several Western jets, and has announced plans to purchase 10 Boeing jets.
"The IL-96-300s we fly today have proved not bad, but we need even better quality," Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, Aeroflot's general director, told Reuters after the news conference.
"The new technology is represented by the IL-96 M/T. I'm a patriot, but I'm also fighting for quality, reliability, regularity and safety, which prompted me to sign this contract."

The Russian aviation industry has complained that Aeroflot's growing use of Western aircraft is crippling domestic aircraft production. Aeroflot officials said aiding domestic production was also a factor in signing the deal.
Shaposhnikov, who was the last defence minister of the Soviet Union, outlined a strategy to use both Western and improved Russian planes in its fleet.

"Our strategy is as follows: our main long-distance jet will be the IL-96, short flights will be on Boeing 737s," he said. Mid range flights will be on the airline's fleet of Russian-built planes, he added.
Alexei Bochkarev, programme manager for Rockwell's Russian operations said the contract for adapting American aviation electronics for Russian planes was worth roughly $50 million.
Officials said the American components in the new planes -- the engines and aviation electronics -- are worth a little more than half of the plane's entire cost.

Officials declined to give a price for the new IL-96 jet, which can carry 318 passengers up to 11,500 km. But Albert Mikhailov, head of the Voronezh factory, told a press conference that it cost half as much as a Boeing jet.
"Now we have a plane that is a competitor to American aircraft," he said, adding that the firm hoped to sell it abroad as well. "It's not any worse than Western planes."
Other aviation officials said the deal would provide steady jobs in an industry hurt by the break up of the Aeroflot monolith and sharp cuts in government subsidies.
"Russian aviation still isn't dead, but it has gone through tough times," Genry Novozhilov, the plane's main designer at the Ilyushin Aviation Complex, said.
"The creation of a Russian-American jet gives the opportunity to each enterprise in their own country to provide jobs."
Aeroflot expects to start flying the new plane in the second half of 1997, pending certification.
